articles.title: I Love Boosters review – supercool outlaw women go shoplifting in Boots Riley’s frantic and funny caper
articles.summary: Demi Moore’s haute-couture maven attracts the attention of a gang of contemporary Robin Hood type clothes robbers in Riley’s fashion biz satire. Here is an entertaining, if very exhausting fantasy-caper about the fashion biz from Boots Riley, a madcap mile-a-minute melee of unadulterated…
body: She plays Christie Smith, a billionaire couture designer who has an office in a trendily designed city block which leans over at an experimental angle. Christie is the object of obsessive attention from “boosters”: supercool young outlaw women who, nettled by her arrogance, shoplift her clothes from upscale stores and sell them on at knockdown Robin Hood prices. They are Corvette (Keke Palmer), Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige), the latter having the superpower of, by holding her breath, turning herself into a white woman who is less likely to be challenged in a store; an interesting metaphor for what Frantz Fanon might have called black skin, white masks.

For all their savvy, the boosters have a soft spot for certain men in their lives, notably a charismatic community leader called Dr Jack (Don Cheadle), who is running a friendship self-help scheme that is actually a fraudulent pyramid scam. And Corvette is entranced by a laidback charmer and oral sex enthusiast played by LaKeith Stansfield, who turns out to be a demonic male succubus.

articles.title: Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romance
articles.summary: Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker.
body: The spirit of mystery author Shirley Jackson is interestingly revived in this peculiar folk-horror romance, adapted from a 2006 story called The Wicker Husband by British writer Ursula Wills. It’s almost funny but not exactly, and almost disturbing but not exactly, occupying a strange and intriguing Venn-diagram overlap between macabre horror and sentimentality. Yet devotees of bucolic British screen-scariness will note that it is, after all, about a wicker man.

The scene is a fabular medieval-effect village that could be in central Europe or England, where there are bizarre patriarchal rituals, like the placing of metal collars on new brides. A depressed middle-aged fisherwoman (fiercely and naturalistically played by Olivia Colman) lives alone in a remote cottage and regularly brings her unappetising tench and gudgeon to market, where she is mocked and bullied by the nasty, closed-minded locals, including Richard E Grant as a lazy and incompetent doctor. Chief among her tormentors is the spiteful tailor’s wife, an elegant, sharp-faced woman played by Elizabeth Debicki.

articles.title: Aliens, Dinosaurs and a Father’s Death: ‘Kefi’ Director Saito Kisin Brings a Surreal Take on Grief to Tokyo
articles.summary: Likely the strangest entry at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, the surreal “Kefi,” the debut feature by cinematographer Saito Kisin, mixes multiple short stories and multiple styles to make sense of the feelings around a complicated relationship with his late father.
body: “Initially, I wanted to do four series of short films and put it together, and that would become a feature,” Saito says. “And those four would all have individual themes. So the first one would be ethics. Second would be hypocrisy. There would be discrimination, and fourth would be life and death.”

The youngest of three brothers, Saito intended to loosely connect the project to his own family, with his shorts following three sisters instead. Then, in 2024, he received news that his father had died.

That news is echoed in the film’s opening. Shortly after a scene in which their absent father speaks about them in narration, an echo from beyond the grave, three sisters – oldest Kyo, middle child Asumi and youngest Kino – learn of his death. Like Saito’s own father, the girls’ father had been separated from the family since their parents’ divorce.
“To tell you the truth, when my father passed, I didn’t feel sad,” Saito says. “Well, the reason being my parents divorced about 10 years ago, I haven’t met him for about 10 or so years.”

articles.title: How did a fishmonger who starred in an adult movie make Rocky? The film about Sylvester Stallone’s amazing triumph
articles.summary: Belittled for his speech and looks, and so short of cash he had to sell his dog, Stallone managed to write and star in one of the greatest boxing movies ever. How does Anthony Ippolito feel about playing his hero?
body: Fifty years ago this December, cinema’s greatest underdog story hit the screen, a tale about a Philadelphia ham-and-egger who takes the world heavyweight boxing champ all the way to the final bell, losing the fight on a judge’s decision but winning the hearts of a nation. That film, of course, was Rocky. Its creation, famously, was no less remarkable an underdog story – one about an out-of-work character actor with the curious name of Sylvester Stallone who wrote his own boxing movie then managed to convince a studio not only to finance it, but also to cast him in the title role. He then went one further than the character he was playing by earning the top prize: a best picture Oscar.

If you thought, half a century on, Rocky’s punching power – its unerring ability to make heroes out of zeroes – has faded, think again. This, after all, is a movie franchise whose stirring qualities are enough to make thousands of people hurtle up all 72 of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s steps every year in homage to its plucky pugilist.

articles.summary: A Thursday morning session at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival, highlighted the Tokyo Broadcasting System (TBS) Group’s initiatives to find global footholds for Japanese content and “inspiring global love for Japan.” Watanabe Shinya, president of the global…
body: The session began by highlighting TBS Group’s global partnerships, particularly with Legendary Entertainment, and with South Korea’s CJ ENM and Japanese streamer U-Next on new joint venture Studio Monowa. Setoguchi spoke about his ongoing interest in Korean programming and content, recalling that 20 years ago he saw a gap between the production capabilities of Korean and Japanese studios, and that, “to my embarrassment,” he had not anticipated the now vast influence of Korean cultural output. “Everywhere you go around the world, K-content and K-drama, they are a part of everybody’s everyday lives,” he said.

Setoguchi said he sees his mission as spreading Japanese content worldwide to a similar extent, and that “instead of working to generate a profit to TBS, I would be working to establish a new genre of J-content.” After calling on the Japanese industry to work together to find global reach for Japanese IP, he spoke about how TBS is connecting with the North American market, noting its $150 million equity investment in Legendary Entertainment earlier this year.

articles.title: ‘Godzilla Minus One’ U.S. Success ‘Wasn’t a Strategy; We Just Tried,’ Says Toho CEO at Tokyo Festival
articles.summary: Japanese studio giant Toho’s North American release of “Godzilla Minus One” was a turning point in the company’s approach to the global market, CEO Matsuoka Hiro said at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Thursday.
body: The result grew out of an opportunity Matsuoka encountered during a U.S. trip. In conversations with exhibitors, he heard that Hollywood studios were not making enough films to meet audience demand. They suggested Toho consider anime; Matsuoka said the discussions helped him recognize the popularity of Japanese animation in the U.S. Since Toho already had “Godzilla,” the company decided to take the franchise to the market itself.

The move was not an obvious one inside Toho. Matsuoka said colleagues were concerned when he proposed the U.S. release, as the company had previously struggled to distribute its films successfully outside Japan. But the film performed well, and, he said, the revenue returned to Toho.
“It was all a coincidence,” Matsuoka said of the opportunity. “It wasn’t a strategy; we just tried.”

For Matsuoka, the experience showed the value of testing new approaches as Toho expands its international business. Toho’s follow-up, Yamazaki Takashi’s “ Godzilla Minus Zero,” will open in Japan on Nov. 3 and in North America on Nov. 6 through Gkids, the U.S. distributor Toho acquired in 2024.

articles.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
articles.summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.
body: Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

articles.title: Actor targets 'scarred villain' screen stereotype
articles.summary: Robert Rhodes says people with scars "experience joy, love and success just like everyone else".
body: An actor is backing a charity's call for more positive roles for performers with scars and visible differences.

Northamptonshire-based Robert Rhodes, who has appeared in Silent Witness and House of the Dragon, said: "The media industry needs to start reflecting the true experience of people with visible difference."

The charity Changing Faces wants the film and TV industry to stop using scars, burns and other visible differences as marks of villainy and has started a petition calling for more positive representation.
One casting agency said visible differences were often used as a shorthand for villainy, but that these casting briefs could be successfully challenged.

articles.title: ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ Ratings Have Never Been Higher. So Why Has This Season Felt Unusually Flat?
articles.summary: Turret trio Maya Jama, James Acaster and King Kenny are firmly under the radar ahead of the endgame, but the jeopardy is severely lacking: "There feels like something is missing with this current run."
body: Its first season aired in October last year and gave us some of the U.K.’s best reality TV in a long time: A traitorous Alan Carr murdering singer-songwriter Paloma Faith in plain sight, Celia Imrie farting in fear during a particularly spooky challenge, and the introduction of the “Big Dog” theory from sportsman Joe Marler, whose hypothesis — that producers would want at least one high-profile name in the turret — has, as we’ve come to find out, endured.

Some may argue that the second season, wrapping up on Friday, boasts an even starrier cast. Twenty-one famous faces were again invited to Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands, where three Traitors are tapped to secretly hunt, lie to, and ultimately murder the Faithful. In between the killings is a series of challenges where participants can contribute to a prize pot for their selected charity, as well as daily roundtables where the group can banish anyone they believe to be a Traitor.

articles.title: Cannes’ Marché du Film, TIFFCOM Commit to Second Edition of Japan IP Market in 2027
articles.summary: The event, running May 14–15 next year, is designed to help international producers navigate Japan’s complex rights landscape and develop adaptations of manga, novels and other IP.
body: TIFFCOM and the Marché du Film will hold a second Japan IP Market at the 2027 Cannes Film Festival, extending this year’s inaugural partnership, which was designed to connect Japanese rights holders with international producers and buyers.

The announcement was made Thursday during TIFFCOM in Tokyo, at the session “Beyond Country of Honour: Building the Next Global Partnerships with Japan.” Alexandra Zakharchenko, the Cannes market’s head of industry programs, was among the speakers.

Its first edition launched in Cannes in May 2026 as part of Japan’s Country of Honor program at the Marché du Film. Participating companies included Kadokawa, Shochiku and Toei, while speakers included Tetsu Fujimura, founder and CEO of Filosophia and an executive producer of Netflix’s live-action One Piece.

The Cannes event is a counterpart to TIFFCOM’s Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake, which launched in 2025 and presents adaptation rights to manga and novels alongside film remake rights. Continuing the partnership gives Japanese companies opportunities to develop international relationships at both the Cannes gathering in May and the Tokyo market in October.
